assertions.text: Output contains a @TableTest annotation
assertions.evidence: Found @TableTest annotation

assertions.text: Each policy threshold (650 for non-seniors, 600 for seniors) is verifiable from the table, in one of two ways: (a) a dedicated policy column (e.g. 'Credit threshold') beside the applicant's score, or (b) boundary rows that bracket it — within one age band, a row that qualifies just above the threshold and a row that fails at/below it, carrying different decisions.
assertions.evidence: Rows 1–2 bracket 650/651 at age 40 (REJECTED/APPROVED); rows 5–6 bracket 600/601 at age 70 (REJECTED/APPROVED). Thresholds are visible from the boundary pairs.

assertions.text: Cell values use concrete domain terms (e.g. '70', '650', 'APPROVED') — not abstract codes like 'CATEGORY_A' or '1'. Boolean true/false is acceptable for yes/no flags when the parameter type is boolean.
assertions.evidence: All values are concrete: ages (40, 64, 65, 70), credit scores (500, 600, 601, 610, 650, 651, 700), results (REJECTED, APPROVED, PENDING_REVIEW), and Boolean stable income (true, false, null).

assertions.text: Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
assertions.evidence: First column(s): "Scenario"

assertions.text: Scenario names describe conditions ('Senior at lower threshold', 'Missing income') — not outcomes ('Approved', 'Rejected').
assertions.evidence: Scenario names describe conditions: 'At the standard threshold, not above it', 'Just above the standard threshold', 'Qualifying score with unstable income', 'Below threshold rejects even with missing income info'.

assertions.text: Column names use domain/business language (e.g. 'Age', 'Credit score', 'Stable income', 'Decision?') — not code identifiers like 'customerAge', 'boolean'.
assertions.evidence: Column headers: 'Age', 'Credit Score', 'Stable Income', 'Result?' — all business language, no code identifiers.

assertions.text: At least one output column name ends with '?' (e.g. 'Decision?' or 'Status?')
assertions.evidence: Question-mark columns: Result?

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
assertions.evidence: 1 method(s) checked — no if/switch/ternary

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: Annotations in correct order: @DisplayName, @Description, @TableTest

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case.
assertions.evidence: 1 @TableTest method name(s) read as descriptive titles (no @DisplayName needed)

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
assertions.evidence: @Description uses text block or is short single-line

assertions.text: The distinct concerns (age→threshold, credit boundary, income status) are each covered, without a monolithic table that re-proves unrelated rules through redundant permutations. A single table is acceptable when the concerns share the same input columns and each is covered by only a row or two.
assertions.evidence: Single table with 11 rows (12 cases via value set). Age boundary (rows 3–4), credit boundary per age band (rows 1–2, 5–6), income status (rows 7–9, 11), precedence (row 11). No redundant cross-multiplication.

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: Age boundary: 2 rows (64/65). Credit boundary: 4 rows (two pairs at different ages). Income status: 3 rows at fixed qualifying score. Precedence: 1 row. Total 11 rows, no redundant permutations.

assertions.text: Age boundary policy, credit score categorisation, and income status are each covered by minimal scenarios. This may be one @TableTest whose rows exercise each concern (boundary pairs for age/credit, income held-constant rows for income status) or separate methods per concern with a combining verdict — both are correct given only a row or two per concern.
assertions.evidence: Age boundary: rows 3–4 (64 vs 65). Credit boundary: rows 1–2 (650 vs 651 at age 40), rows 5–6 (600 vs 601 at age 70). Income status: rows 7–9 hold age 40, score 700 fixed, vary income (true/false/null).

assertions.text: Scenario names and @Description text do not restate values the table already shows. The assertion FAILS if either: (1) a scenario name contains a literal value that also appears in an input cell of the same row (e.g. scenario 'Age 35, score 700' beside Age and Credit score columns holding 35 and 700); or (2) @Description states a fixed value for an input that is already a column in that table.
assertions.evidence: @Description does not restate 650, 600, 65, or any column value. It states interpretive assumptions ('below-threshold scores are rejected regardless of income is read to cover missing (null) income too') that the rows prove but prose cannot.

assertions.text: The effect of stable income on the outcome is visible from table rows, not merely implied. The assertion PASSES if some single @TableTest table contains two rows that differ in the stable-income column (or equivalent) while holding the credit score and age columns equal, and those two rows carry different expected decisions.
assertions.evidence: Rows 7–8 hold age 40, credit score 700 fixed; row 7 has stable income true → APPROVED, row 8 has stable income null → PENDING_REVIEW. Row 9 also holds age 70, score 610 fixed, income null → PENDING_REVIEW (income effect visible).

assertions.text: The build file (build.gradle) includes org.tabletest:tabletest-junit as a test dependency
assertions.evidence: Build file contains tabletest-junit

assertions.text: Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. Judge each @TableTest table independently; the assertion FAILS if any table meets any of these conditions: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row.
assertions.evidence: Result column varies: REJECTED (rows 1, 3, 5, 10, 11), APPROVED (rows 2, 4, 6), PENDING_REVIEW (rows 8, 9). No row's result is a copy of an input cell. A fixed-value implementation would fail rows with different results.

assertions.text: A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body.
assertions.evidence: Table includes boundary rows (650/651 for age 40, 600/601 for age 65+), three income variations at fixed qualifying score (700, age 40), and precedence row (500 score with null income → REJECTED). All thresholds, age effect, and income rules are visible from column headers and cell values.

assertions.text: Each @DisplayName states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on.
assertions.evidence: The @Description states 'Standard applicants are approved above a credit score of 650; senior applicants (age 65+) are approved above a lower threshold of 600.' Striking 'the code under test' leaves 'applicants are approved above 650/600' — a domain rule, not what the evaluator does. The description restates policy thresholds already carried by the table rows.
